metadata.title: The Clock Needs a Rock.
metadata.clock: narration (Kokoro af_bella) - per-beat mp3 durations are MEASURED, never estimated

metadata.target_runtime: Under 3:00 BY DESIGN. 426 words against the measured 0.3744 s/word of Ep. 17 (159.49 s / 426 w) predicts 159.5 s = 2:39.5, leaving ~20 s of margin. The words-only model has run +-5-10% with no consistent sign across Ep. 06-17, so the worst observed overshoot (+10.4%) still lands at 2:56.
metadata.purpose: Ep. 18 of the AI in Astronomy & Space Science series, from weekly_stem_videos/ideas.md Astronomy topic 18 (dating planets by their craters). The episode SPLITS the problem rather than answering it once: crater DETECTION is perception and belongs to AI; crater DATING is a calibration anchored to radiometrically dated returned samples, and no detector has ever moved it. The hinge is that both halves wear the same word, 'counting'.
metadata.boundary: ideas.md Notes governs Eps. 16-28: each covers a subject none of 01-15 touch, and none is about asteroids. Ep. 08 (asteroid-impact-warning) detects and tracks objects BEFORE they strike, for planetary defence. Ep. 18 never looks at an object in flight: every crater here is already on the ground and the only question asked of it is how long it has been there. Ep. 06 (mars-rover-autonomy) drives a vehicle; nothing here is driven. B03 states the frame out loud.
metadata.color_semantics: Claude fidelity palette, and the map NEVER flips across the six plates. Terracotta #D97757 is THE COUNT - the measurement, the thing a better detector changes. Ink #3D3929 is THE CLOCK - the chronology curve and the dated rocks that hold it up. That is the episode's whole argument rendered as two colours, so cost.png literally shows terracotta passing through ink. Ghost #B9B4A0 and faint are scaffolding only (frames, axes, the empty gap) and never text. One local convention, taught in-beat at B05: in spread.png a FILLED crater is one every analyst marked and an OPEN one is contested. Accented text is #A44A32.
metadata.distinct_from_earlier_episodes: Ep. 10 (classifying-supernovae) triages transients that are still changing; Ep. 17 (scheduling-the-night) allocates future exposures. Both decide what to DO next. Ep. 18 decides what already happened, to ground that has not changed in a billion years - the only episode in the series whose subject cannot be observed twice. No plate, number or source is shared with any earlier episode.
metadata.note: The episode's claim is falsifiable and the falsification SHIPS as beat B10: the Chang'e-5 recalibration moved the Neukum curve by at most ~0.24 Gyr, so crater counting was never wildly wrong. That weakens the headline and is stated on screen rather than omitted. B06 ships the same way: the 92% recall is post-processing, and the raw CNN number (57%) is placed beside it.

assets.plate_rule: plates carry IMAGERY ONLY - no text, ticks or legend. Every label is placed by scenes.py OUTSIDE the plate, because GATE B is nearly blind to a plate's interior.

beats.narration_text: Hi, I'm Om Mali. This video is about how we date a planet's surface by counting its craters, and why AI counts them far better than we can, but cannot date them at all.

show.event: the composer types the ask on the cream stage
the send button arms in terracotta
running indicator: reading the age off ground nobody has sampled
three result lines land in order, the third one landing on 'cannot'

props.command: Nobody has visited most of the Moon or Mars. We still quote their surface ages in billions of years. Where does that number actually come from?
props.runningText: counting craters on ground nobody has sampled...
output: Count craters per km^2 - denser ground is older ground
Read the age off a curve calibrated by DATED ROCKS
AI can do the counting. It cannot move the curve.

beats.narration_text: Eighteen episodes on where AI's answers come from. This one splits down the middle. AI owns the counting. It does not own the number the counting turns into.

show.event: OM MALI writes in, terracotta hairline underlines it
role line fades in: Humanitarians AI - presenter
series line and corner bug land early, so the lower band is never empty
a card draws beside it and SPLITS down a centre rule
left half fills terracotta: COUNTING / AI owns this
right half stays ink: THE NUMBER / it does not

beats.narration_text: Here's the whole idea. More craters means older ground. Turning a count into years needs a curve, and that curve is held up by dated rocks. A better counter moves the measurement. Only a rock moves the curve.

show.event: a card draws on the cream stage
line one types: MORE CRATERS MEANS OLDER GROUND, sub: density is the measurement
line two: YEARS NEED A CURVE, sub: and the curve needs dated rocks
line three lands in the accent and is UNDERLINED: ONLY A ROCK MOVES THE CURVE
closer: a better counter only moves the measurement

beats.narration_text: The rule is embarrassingly simple. Ground that sat there longer got hit more. Same area, same instrument: fourteen craters left, eighty right. One billion years, against three and a half.

show.event: title bar and chrome; surface.png fades up, both patches at once
left patch label lands: 1.0 Ga
its counter runs up to 14
right patch label lands: 3.5 Ga
its counter runs up to 80 - visibly longer to climb
closer: every crater here is already on the ground

beats.narration_text: So you count. One Mars catalogue holds three hundred eighty-four thousand craters, built by hand. Go smaller and the population runs to tens of millions. Hands stop here.

show.event: chrome; pile.png fades up with its decade rails, bars empty of meaning until labelled
a 'x10 per rail' note lands under the axis so nobody reads it as linear
row one labels: 7,048 - the training set
row two labels: 384,343 - catalogued BY HAND (Robbins & Hynek 2012)
row three labels: ~10 million-plus - 10 m to 1 km on Mars
the third row's label turns accented on 'hands stop here'

beats.narration_text: And hands disagree. Give expert counters the same image and their totals differ by up to forty-five percent. The big craters are unanimous. The small ones are genuinely arguable.

show.event: chrome; spread.png fades up - one patch, craters filled and open
the +-45% figure lands large beside it, cited small: Robbins et al. 2014
legend row one: FILLED = every analyst marked it
legend row two: OPEN = contested
closer: the disagreement is all in the small ones

beats.narration_text: So automate it. DeepMoon, a network reading lunar elevation, recovers ninety-two percent of known craters, and forty-two percent of what it found was new. Perception is exactly AI's job.

show.event: chrome; a two-row bar frame draws, no plate - this beat is numbers
bar one grows to 92% and holds: recall, AFTER post-processing
bar two grows to 57% beneath it, ghosted: the raw network, placed so the headline cannot stand alone
a third figure lands in the accent: 42% of what it returned was NEW
closer lands: this half is perception - and perception is AI's

beats.narration_text: Now the other half. Density isn't years. It's a lookup on this curve, flat through the middle, explosive at the old end. On ancient ground, ninety-six percent of the craters landed in the first six hundred million years.

show.event: chrome; curve.png fades up, axes labelled OUTSIDE the plate
y-axis label lands: craters per km^2 (log)
x-axis label lands: age, billions of years
a bracket marks the long flat middle: a slow, steady clock
a second bracket marks the steep old end: the early bombardment
96% lands in the accent against the steep end

beats.narration_text: So run that forty-five percent through the curve. On three-and-a-half-billion-year-old ground it costs sixteen percent of the answer. On one-billion-year-old ground, the same error costs ninety percent.

show.event: chrome; cost.png fades up - curve above, the two age bars below
the 3.5 Ga bar is called out: 16% of the answer
the 1.0 Ga bar is called out in the accent: 90%
a note lands under the bars: the SAME counting error, both times
closer: consistency buys the most on young ground

beats.narration_text: Here's what the curve is nailed to: rocks somebody flew home and dated. Between one and three billion years, there were none. Chang'e-5 landed in that hole.

show.event: chrome; anchors.png fades up, time axis labelled outside the plate
the old cluster is labelled: Apollo + Luna
the young cluster is labelled: a few dated craters
the empty middle is labelled in the accent: 1 - 3 Ga, NO ANCHOR
the Chang'e-5 marker lands in the hole, 2026 note beneath

beats.narration_text: Counting that plain gave a window one-point-four billion years wide. The returned basalt gave eight million. And it moved the curve by at most a quarter-billion years. Counting was never wrong, just loose.

show.event: chrome; a wide terracotta bar draws: the counted window, 1,400 Myr
it COLLAPSES to a single ink tick: the rock, 8 Myr
the ratio lands between them: 175x tighter
the counterweight types in beneath, ghosted, not hidden: the new anchor moved the curve by at most 0.24 Gyr
closer in the accent: not wrong - loose

beats.narration_text: So: when not to learn it. Automate the measurement. That's perception, and machines win on consistency alone. Don't automate the calibration. No detector has ever moved that curve. A rock did.

show.event: the artifact page opens on the cream stage
heading lands: When not to learn it
the five lines land in order, the last one holding

props.artifactTitle: The Clock Needs a Rock - one page
artifactLines: AUTOMATE the measurement: finding craters is perception, and it scales.
Machines win on CONSISTENCY, not just speed - experts differ by up to 45%.
DON'T automate the calibration. The density-to-age curve is not in the pixels.
A model trained on crater counts can only repeat the curve it was handed.
Every anchor on that curve is a rock somebody flew home and dated.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this: take a measurement I trust in my own work. Separate what's measured from what it's calibrated against, and tell me which one I've never checked. Whatever it names, that's your curve.

show.event: the composer returns, greeting fixed to 'Your turn.'
the prompt types itself while the voice reads it aloud
running indicator: paste this into Claude...
two result lines land: what to look for in the answer

props.command: Take a measurement I trust in my own work. Separate what is MEASURED from what it is CALIBRATED AGAINST, and tell me which of the two I have never checked.
output: Expect it to find the calibration you inherited and never audited
A number is only as good as the thing it was compared to

beats.narration_text: The Clock Needs a Rock. Claude for Astronomy, episode eighteen.
